claim: Ubiquitous deletion of Tek led to embryonic lethality by E10.5
source: Ubiquitous deletion of Tek led to embryonic lethality by E10.5 (Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C), as previously reported (Sato et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 1A–C and cited literature (Sato et al., 1995)

claim: No veins were detected in the head or somite regions of the Tek null embryos at E9.5
source: As shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E, no veins (arrows) were detected in the head or somite regions of the Tek null embryos at E9.5, unlike in the littermate control embryos.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1A,B and Figure 1—figure supplement 1D,E

claim: Tie2 expression in the E9.5 embryos was higher in veins than in arteries
source: Interestingly, Tie2 expression in the E9.5 embryos was higher in veins than in arteries (arrowhead, Figure 1B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1B

claim: Venogenesis was disrupted in both Tek−/iUCKO and Tek−/iECKO mutant embryos when Tek deletion was induced at E10.5–12.5
source: Analysis of veins in skin at E15.5 showed that venogenesis was disrupted in both types of mutant embryos, in which Tek deletion was induced by intraperitoneal injections of tamoxifen into pregnant mice at E10.5–12.5 (Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1C–E and Figure 1—figure supplement 2A

claim: Defective vein formation was observed in the skin of E17.5 Tek−/iUCKO embryos when Tek deletion was induced at E12.5–14.5
source: In addition, defective vein formation was also observed in the skin of E17.5 Tek−/iUCKO embryos when Tek deletion was induced at E12.5–14.5 (Figure 1F).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1F

claim: Veins were detected in mesentery but did not align properly with the arteries in Tek mutant embryos
source: Interestingly, veins were detected in mesentery, but unlike in littermate controls, they did not align properly with the arteries (Figure 1—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 2B

claim: Lymphatic vessels were present in the skin of Tek−/iECKO mutant mice but became dilated
source: We found that lymphatic vessels were present in the skin of Tek−/iECKO mutant mice, but became dilated (Figure 1—figure supplement 3).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 1—figure supplement 3

claim: The level of Tie2 mRNA in the lung was 0.25 ± 0.02 in Tek−/iUCKO compared with 1.0 ± 0.11 in Tek+/iUCKO mice
source: The level of Tie2 mRNA in the lung was 0.25 ± 0.02 in Tek−/iUCKO (n = 4), as compared with that of the heterozygous mice (Tek+/iUCKO: 1.0 ± 0.11, n = 4).
evidence: Supported by real-time RT-PCR data

claim: The decrease of Tie2 in the Tek−/iUCKO and Tek−/iECKO mice resulted in a significant decrease of retinal vascularization
source: Interestingly, the decrease of Tie2 in the Tek−/iUCKO and Tek−/iECKO mice resulted in a significant decrease of retinal vascularization, as indicated by a lower vascular index (Figure 2C–F).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2C–F

claim: The vascularization index in Tek−/iUCKO mice was 61.95 ± 10.79 compared to 100.0 ± 10.94 in controls (p<0.0001)
source: Quantification of the vascularization index (ratio of vascularized area to total retina area normalized against the littermate controls) after ubiquitous (E, Tek−/iUCKO: 61.95 ± 10.79, n = 12; Control: 100.0 ± 10.94, n = 12; p<0.0001)
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2E

claim: The vascularization index in Tek−/iECKO mice was 80.69 ± 11.13 compared to 100.0 ± 3.77 in controls (p<0.0015)
source: EC-specific deletion (F, Tek-/iECKO: 80.69 ± 11.13, n = 5; Control: 100.0 ± 3.77, n = 7; p<0.0015).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2F

claim: Tie2 expression is downregulated in tip endothelial cells
source: Note that Tie2 expression is downregulated in tip endothelial cells (asterisk in C and D)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: Tie2 expression is low in newly formed retinal arteries when compared with veins
source: and also low in newly formed retinal arteries (arrowhead in C and D) when compared with veins (arrow in C and D).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2C and D

claim: There was a significant increase of vascular density at the front of the venous segments of Tek−/iUCKO mutants compared with controls at P7
source: In spite of the decreased vascular index in retina, there was a significant increase of vascular density at the front of the venous but not arterial segments of Tek−/iUCKO mutants compared with controls at P7 (Figure 2G–J).
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2G–J

claim: Blood vessel density in the distal retinal venous segments was 16.91 ± 0.77 in Tek−/iUCKO compared to 14.07 ± 1.54 in controls (p=0.0014)
source: Quantification of blood vessel density in the distal retinal venous (I, X 104 μm2/grid; Tek−/iUCKO: 16.91 ± 0.77, n = 6; Control: 14.07 ± 1.54, n = 8; p=0.0014)
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2I

claim: Blood vessel density in the distal retinal arterial segments was 10.45 ± 2.47 in Tek−/iUCKO compared to 10.16 ± 0.76 in controls (p=0.7571)
source: and arterial segments (J, X 104 μm2/grid; Tek−/iUCKO: 10.45 ± 2.47, n = 6; Control: 10.16 ± 0.76, n = 8; p=0.7571) in Tek mutants compared with control mice.
evidence: Supported by quantification data shown in Figure 2J

claim: There was a significantly decreased phosphorylation of the Dok-2 docking protein in the lungs of Tek−/iUCKO mice compared with controls
source: Biochemical analysis revealed a significantly decreased phosphorylation of the Dok-2 docking protein (pDok2 / beta-actin, Tek−/iUCKO: 0.38 ± 0.25, n = 6; Control: 1.0 ± 0.24, n = 6; p=0.0014; pDok2 / tDok2, Tek−/iUCKO: 0.52 ± 0.10, n = 3; Control: 1.0 ± 0.21, n = 3; p=0.024)
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2K,L

claim: There was an increase of Erk1/2 phosphorylation in the lungs of Tek−/iUCKO mice compared with controls
source: but an increase of Erk1/2 phosphorylation (pERK1/2 / tERK1/2, Tek−/iUCKO: 1.71 ± 0.70, n = 10; Control: 1.0 ± 0.30, n = 9; p=0.012) in the lungs of Tek−/iUCKO mice compared with controls (Figure 2K,L).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 2K,L

claim: The total Dok-2 protein level decreased in the mutant mice after Tie2 reduction compared with that of the littermate control
source: It is worth noting that the total Dok-2 protein level also decreased in the mutant mice after Tie2 reduction compared with that of the littermate control.
evidence: Inferred from Western blot analysis

claim: No obvious defects were observed in the retinal blood vessels of TekFlox/−;Vav-iCre mutant mice
source: As Tie2 is also expressed by some hematopoietic cells, we generated mutant mice with Tek deletion in blood cells (TekFlox/−;Vav-iCre) (de Boer et al., 2003). No obvious defects were observed in the retinal blood vessels of the mutant mice (Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 2—figure supplement 2A,B and cited literature (de Boer et al., 2003)

claim: The morphology of veins was severely disrupted at P15 in mice with postnatal Tek deletion
source: The abnormal angiogenesis along the retinal veins was also seen at P11 in mice with postnatal Tek deletion, and the morphology of veins was severely disrupted at P15 (Figure 3B and C, arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3B and C

claim: Vein degeneration was accompanied by the formation of haemangioma-like vascular tufts by P21
source: Vein degeneration was accompanied by the formation of haemangioma-like vascular tufts by P21 (Figure 3D, arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3D

claim: The massive angiogenic vascular growth occurred mainly in the first layer of retinal vessels of Tek−/iUCKO mice
source: The massive angiogenic vascular growth occurred mainly in the first layer of retinal vessels of Tek−/iUCKO mice (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by cross-sectional analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: Tek−/iUCKO mutant mice at P21 exhibited little blood vessel growth towards the deep layers of retina
source: In contrast to wildtype littermate control mice, Tek−/iUCKOmutant mice at P21 exhibited little blood vessel growth towards the deep layers of retina (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by cross-sectional analysis shown in Figure 3E

claim: Vessels in the vascular tufts in the Tek−/iUCKO mice had lumens and were covered with NG2+ pericytes
source: Vessels in the vascular tufts in the Tek−/iUCKO mice had lumens and were covered with NG2+ pericytes (Figure 3E).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3E

claim: Tek deletion at P5-8 resulted in a similar but milder vascular phenotype
source: Furthermore, Tek deletion at a later stage (P5-8) resulted in a similar but milder vascular phenotype (Figure 3F, arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3F

claim: Vascular tufts were not observed in Tek−/iECKO mice at different time points
source: For comparison, we also performed the analysis of retinal blood vasculature at different time points with Tek-/iECKO mice, but did not observe the formation of vascular tufts.
evidence: Based on experimental observations

claim: The lack of vascular tuft formation in Tek−/iECKO mice may be due to the lower efficiency of Tek gene deletion
source: This may be due to the lower efficiency of Tek gene deletion as discussed above.
evidence: Inferred from deletion efficiency data

claim: Tie2 attenuation led to a significant decrease in body weight gain as measured until three weeks postnatally
source: Tie2 attenuation (Tamoxifen treatment at P1–4) led to a significant decrease in body weight gain as measured until three weeks postnatally: control mice: P7, 3.68 ± 0.48 g (n = 24); P9, 3.97 ± 0.34 g (n = 6); P11, 5.73 ± 1.37 g (n = 16); P21, 8.40 ± 1.29 g (n = 8); and Tek−/iUCKO mutants: P7, 2.71 ± 0.51 g (n = 24; p<0.0001); P9, 3.13 ± 0.57 g (n = 3; p=0.0252); P11, 4.09 ± 0.81 g (n = 11; p=0.0015); P21, 5.87 ± 1.30 g (n = 6; p=0.0035).
evidence: Supported by body weight measurements shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 1

claim: Postnatal attenuation of Tie2 did not produce an obvious effect on blood vessels in tail skin at P7
source: Unlike in the retina, postnatal attenuation of Tie2 did not produce an obvious effect on blood vessels in tail skin at P7 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2A)
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2A

claim: Postnatal attenuation of Tie2 did not produce an obvious effect on blood vessels in ear skin at P21
source: or ear skin at P21 (Figure 3—figure supplement 2B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 3—figure supplement 2B

claim: Veins in ear skin were found to be tortuous in 2.5 month-old adult Tek−/iUCKO mutants compared with the control mice
source: However, veins in ear skin were found to be tortuous in 2.5 month-old adult mutants compared with the control mice (Figure 4A, arrows).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4A

claim: Tek transcript level remained low in Tek−/iUCKO mice at 2.5 months (0.26 ± 0.14 compared to 1.0 ± 0.28 in controls)
source: The expression analysis by real-time RT-PCR revealed that Tek transcript level remained low in Tek−/iUCKO mice at this stage (Tek−/iUCKO: 0.26 ± 0.14, n = 5; Control: 1.0 ± 0.28, n = 5).
evidence: Supported by real-time RT-PCR data

claim: Venous tortuosity was observed in retinas of Tek−/iUCKO mice at the adult stage (2.5 month-old) while the increased angiogenesis along the retinal veins regressed
source: Interestingly, the venous tortuosity was also observed in retinas of Tek−/iUCKO mice at the adult stage (2.5 month-old) while the increased angiogenesis along the retinal veins regressed (Figure 4B).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 4B

claim: Tie2 has an important role in the postnatal maintenance of veins
source: The findings suggest that Tie2 has an important role in the postnatal maintenance of veins.
evidence: Inferred from the observation of venous tortuosity in adult mutants

claim: Tie2 attenuation led to the alteration of venous EC identity as shown by the change of EC marker expression
source: Mechanistically, we found that Tie2 attenuation led to the alteration of venous EC identity as shown by the change of EC marker expression (Figure 5A, and Table 1).
evidence: Supported by expression analysis shown in Figure 5A and Table 1

claim: Transcript levels of the venous marker APJ and EphB4 were decreased in the retinas and lungs of Tek−/iUCKO mice compared with littermate controls
source: Transcript levels of the venous marker APJ and EphB4 were decreased, whereas COUP-TFII mRNA level was unaltered in the retinas and lungs of Tek−/iUCKO mice compared with littermate controls (P7; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A

claim: COUP-TFII mRNA level was unaltered in the retinas and lungs of Tek−/iUCKO mice compared with littermate controls
source: Transcript levels of the venous marker APJ and EphB4 were decreased, whereas COUP-TFII mRNA level was unaltered in the retinas and lungs of Tek−/iUCKO mice compared with littermate controls (P7; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A

claim: There was a significant increase of arterial and angiogenic sprout marker Dll4 transcripts in the lungs of Tek−/iUCKO mice
source: Furthermore, there was a significant increase of arterial and angiogenic sprout marker Dll4 transcripts in the lungs (Figure 5A) (Hellström et al., 2007).
evidence: Supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A and cited literature (Hellström et al., 2007)

claim: Tie2 reduction induced Dll4 expression in retinal veins
source: Consistently, Tie2 reduction induced Dll4 expression in retinal veins (P9; Figure 5B, arrows point to veins in dotted regions), which were negative by immunostaining for Dll4 in littermate control mice (Figure 5C).
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data shown in Figure 5B and 5C

claim: There was no significant alteration of other arterial markers including NRP1, EphrinB2 and NOTCH1 in Tek−/iUCKO mice at P7
source: There was no significant alteration of other arterial markers including NRP1, EphrinB2 and NOTCH1 (P7; Figure 5A).
evidence: Supported by real-time RT-PCR data shown in Figure 5A

claim: Venous genes EphB4 and APJ were significantly decreased in lung of Tek−/iUCKO mice compared with controls at the adult stage
source: Consistently, we found that venous genes were significantly decreased in lung of Tek−/iUCKO mice compared with controls (EphB4, Tek−/iUCKO: 0.52 ± 0.29, n = 5; Control: 1.0 ± 0.18, n = 5; APJ, Tek−/iUCKO: 0.22 ± 0.22, n = 5; Control: 1.0 ± 0.25, n = 5).
evidence: Supported by real-time RT-PCR data

claim: There was a trend of reduction in the arterial gene expression in Tek−/iUCKO mice at the adult stage
source: Interestingly, there was also a trend of reduction in the arterial gene expression in Tek−/iUCKO mice (Ephrin B2, Tek−/iUCKO: 0.71 ± 0.32, n = 5; Control: 1.0 ± 0.23, n = 5; Dll4, Tek−/iUCKO: 0.70 ± 0.36, n = 5; Control: 1.0 ± 0.21, n = 5)
evidence: Supported by real-time RT-PCR data

claim: Tie2 retardation may affect arteries at later stages
source: suggesting that Tie2 retardation may also affect arteries at later stages.
evidence: Inferred from the trend of reduction in arterial gene expression

claim: Tie2 deletion led to a decrease of Akt phosphorylation (Ser473)
source: Tie2 deletion led to a decrease of Akt phosphorylation (Ser473, Figure 6A,B).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A,B

claim: COUP-TFII protein was significantly decreased in lung and liver tissues of Tek mutant mice
source: Interestingly, COUP-TFII protein was significantly decreased in lung and liver tissues of Tek mutant mice (Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B), although COUP-TFII mRNA level was not altered, as shown above.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6A,B and Figure 6—figure supplement 1A,B

claim: COUP-TFII protein was decreased when Tie2 was reduced by siRNA mediated knockdown in cultured HUVECs
source: This was further verified in cultured HUVECs, where COUP-TFII protein was decreased when Tie2 was reduced by siRNA mediated knockdown (Figure 6C–D).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6C–D

claim: COUP-TFII protein was significantly increased by the COMP-Ang1 stimulation of Tie2/Akt pathway
source: Consistently, COUP-TFII protein was significantly increased by the COMP-Ang1 stimulation of Tie2/Akt pathway (Figure 6E–F).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6E–F

claim: COUP-TFII protein was significantly reduced 6 hr or 12 hr after treatment with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002
source: COUP-TFII protein was significantly reduced 6 hr or 12 hr after treatment with the PI3K inhibitor LY294002 (Figure 6G,H; LY-3h: 1.11 ± 0.39, n = 5; LY-6h: 0.62 ± 0.12, n = 5; LY-12h: 0.39 ± 0.13, n = 5; values from five independent experiments normalized against control at three time points respectively).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6G,H

claim: There was a significant decrease of COUP-TFII after Akt inhibition with MK2206 at the 12 hr time point
source: This was further confirmed with the Akt inhibitor MK2206, and there was a significant decrease of COUP-TFII after Akt inhibition at the 12 hr time point (Figure 6I,J; MK-3h: 1.32 ± 0.47, n = 7; MK-6h: 0.75 ± 0.31, n = 7; MK-12h: 0.23 ± 0.18, n = 7; values from seven independent experiments normalized against control at three time points respectively).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6I,J

claim: The decrease of COUP-TFII protein by the Akt inhibition could be reverted by the treatment with a proteasome inhibitor MG132
source: Furthermore, the decrease of COUP-TFII protein by the Akt inhibition could be reverted by the treatment with a proteasome inhibitor MG132 (Figure 6K–L).
evidence: Supported by Western blot data shown in Figure 6K–L

claim: The Tie2 signaling pathway controls vein specification via Akt-mediated regulation of COUP-TFII protein stability
source: These findings suggest that the Tie2 signaling pathway controls vein specification via Akt-mediated regulation of COUP-TFII protein stability (Figure 6M).
evidence: Inferred from multiple experimental results showing Tie2/Akt regulation of COUP-TFII protein

claim: Tie2 is more expressed in veins than arteries in early embryos and in retina of neonate mice with the newly formed arteries expressing low level of Tie2
source: We show here that Tie2 is more expressed in veins than arteries in early embryos and in retina of neonate mice with the newly formed arteries expressing low level of Tie2.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data presented in the Results section

claim: Tie2 is downregulated in the sprouting tip endothelial cells as observed in retinal angiogenesis
source: Interestingly, Tie2 is also downregulated in the sprouting tip endothelial cells as observed in retinal angiogenesis in this study and also by others (Augustin et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by data in this study and cited literature (Augustin et al., 2009)

claim: Vein-derived endothelial tip cells contribute to the emerging arteries during mouse retinal vascularization and in zebrafish fin regeneration
source: It has been recently reported that vein-derived endothelial tip cells contribute to the emerging arteries during mouse retinal vascularization and also in zebrafish fin regeneration (Xu et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Xu et al., 2014)

claim: The downregulation of Tie2 may be required for the initial establishment of an arterial EC identity
source: This suggests that the downregulation of Tie2 may be required for the initial establishment of an arterial EC identity.
evidence: Inferred from the observation that Tie2 is downregulated in tip cells that contribute to arteries

claim: Tie2 absence or insufficiency by gene targeting disrupts venogenesis during embryogenesis and postnatal development
source: Consistently, we have demonstrated in this study that Tie2 absence or insufficiency by gene targeting disrupts venogenesis during embryogenesis and postnatal development.
evidence: Supported by multiple experimental results presented in the study

claim: Tie2 participates in the determination of venous EC identity via Akt-mediated regulation of COUP-TFII protein stability
source: At the molecular level, we have found that Tie2 participates in the determination of venous EC identity, which may act via Akt-mediated regulation of COUP-TFII protein stability.
evidence: Inferred from biochemical and molecular data presented in the study

claim: Tie2/Akt signaling counterbalances VEGFR2/MAPK pathway in arteriovenous specification during the vascular development
source: This implies that Tie2/Akt signaling counterbalances VEGFR2/MAPK pathway in arteriovenous specification during the vascular development.
evidence: Inferred from the findings and consistent with previous literature on Akt in venous development

claim: Cardiomyocyte derived Ang1 is required for the subepicardial coronary vein formation
source: The findings are consistent with previous literature on the role of Akt in venous development, and with the recent report that cardiomyocyte derived Ang1 is required for the subepicardial coronary vein formation (Deng et al., 2013; Ren et al., 2010; Zimmermann and Moelling, 1999; Lamont and Childs, 2006; Arita et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Deng et al., 2013; Ren et al., 2010; Zimmermann and Moelling, 1999; Lamont and Childs, 2006; Arita et al., 2014)

claim: The disruption of cutaneous vein development during embryogenesis is likely to be a cell-autonomous effect resulting from the deletion of Tie2 in endothelial cells
source: This suggests that the disruption of cutaneous vein development during embryogenesis is likely to be a cell-autonomous effect resulting from the deletion of Tie2 in endothelial cells.
evidence: Inferred from the comparison of different Cre deletor lines

claim: Reduction of Tie2 mediated signals in ECs and/or other Tie2 expressing cells may be implicated in the vascular pathologies associated with retinal neovascularization
source: As retinal neovascularization is one of the frequent causes of vision loss in patients with proliferative diabetic retinopathy and neovascular age-related macular degeneration (Gariano and Gardner, 2005), these data suggests that reduction of Tie2 mediated signals in ECs and / or other Tie2 expressing cells may be implicated in the vascular pathologies.
evidence: Inferred from the vascular tuft formation in Tie2 mutants and cited literature (Gariano and Gardner, 2005)

claim: COUP-TFII has been shown to regulate venous EC identity as well as lymphatic EC specification
source: In the vascular system, COUP-TFII has been shown to regulate venous EC identity as well as lymphatic EC specification (You et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2010; Srinivasan et al., 2010).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (You et al., 2005; Lin et al., 2010; Srinivasan et al., 2010)

claim: At the transcription level, COUP-TFII is regulated by several factors/pathways including NOTCH and SOX7/18
source: At the transcription level, COUP-TFII is regulated by several factors / pathways including NOTCH and SOX7/18 (Swift et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Swift et al., 2014)

claim: COUP-TFII protein but not its mRNA level is significantly reduced in genetically engineered mouse model targeting Tek
source: In this study, we have found that COUP-TFII protein but not its mRNA level is significantly reduced in genetically engineered mouse model targeting Tek.
evidence: Supported by Western blot and RT-PCR data presented in the study

claim: Akt is a strong candidate mediating Tie2 signals in the regulation of COUP-TFII protein stability
source: Based on the evidence obtained from the biochemical analysis with cultured endothelial cells, we propose that Akt is a strong candidate mediating Tie2 signals in this process.
evidence: Inferred from biochemical analysis with cultured endothelial cells

claim: The requirement of Tie2 for vein development differs between the skin and mesentery
source: In addition, we have also found that the requirement of Tie2 for vein development differs between the skin and mesentery.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data showing different phenotypes in skin and mesentery

claim: When Tie2 levels were reduced by gene targeting, veins were mostly undetectable in the skin, but displayed only abnormal arterial-venous alignment in the mesentery
source: When Tie2 levels were reduced by gene targeting, veins were mostly undetectable in the skin, but displayed only abnormal arterial-venous alignment in the mesentery.
evidence: Supported by immunostaining data presented in the study

claim: The cutaneous veins are more sensitive to the loss of Tie2 mediated signals, or venogenesis occurs earlier in the mesentery than in the skin
source: It is possible that the cutaneous veins are more sensitive to the loss of Tie2 mediated signals, or that venogenesis occurs earlier in the mesentery than in the skin.
evidence: Speculative explanation for the observed differences between skin and mesentery

claim: The abnormal arteriovenous alignment in Tek mutants resembled that of the APJ deficient mice
source: The abnormal arteriovenous alignment resembled that of the APJ deficient mice (Kidoya et al., 2015)
evidence: Supported by comparison with cited literature (Kidoya et al., 2015)

claim: A significant reduction of APJ in the Tek mutants suggests that APJ acts downstream of Tie2 in the regulation of venous patterning
source: and a significant reduction of APJ in the Tek mutants suggests that APJ acts downstream of Tie2 in the regulation of venous patterning.
evidence: Inferred from the reduction of APJ in Tek mutants and the similar phenotype to APJ deficient mice

claim: Both the total and phosphorylated Dok-2 decreased significantly after Tie2 attenuation
source: Interestingly, we have also found that both the total and phosphorylated Dok-2 decreased significantly after Tie2 attenuation in this study.
evidence: Supported by Western blot data presented in the study

claim: Dok family members have been shown to negatively regulate ERK1/2 activation
source: As Dok family members have been shown to negatively regulate ERK1/2 activation (Honma et al., 2006)
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Honma et al., 2006)

claim: The decrease of Dok-2 may lead to the increase of retinal angiogenesis as detected in mice with Tie2 reduction by gene targeting
source: the decrease of Dok-2 may lead to the increase of retinal angiogenesis as detected in mice with Tie2 reduction by gene targeting.
evidence: Inferred from the negative regulation of ERK1/2 by Dok-2 and the observed increase in angiogenesis

claim: Enhancement of Tie2 signaling via the inhibition of VE-PTP has been shown to stabilize blood vessels and suppress retinal angiogenesis in mouse models of ischemia-induced retinal neovascularization
source: Consistently, enhancement of Tie2 signaling via the inhibition of VE-PTP has been shown to stabilize blood vessels and suppress retinal angiogenesis in mouse models of ischemia-induced retinal neovascularization (Shen et al., 2014b).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Shen et al., 2014b)

claim: Dok2, via directly interacting with Tie2, mediated Tie2 pathway in endothelial cell migration
source: Furthermore, in experiments using HEK 293 T or endothelial cells overexpressing Dok2, it was found that Dok2, via directly interacting with Tie2, mediated Tie2 pathway in endothelial cell migration (Saharinen et al., 2008; Master et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Saharinen et al., 2008; Master et al., 2001)

claim: Decreased Dok-2 activation in Tek mutants may account for the suppression of horizontal and vertical blood vessel growth during retinal vascular network formation
source: Decreased Dok-2 activation in Tek mutants may also account for the suppression of horizontal and vertical blood vessel growth during retinal vascular network formation.
evidence: Inferred from the role of Dok-2 in Tie2 signaling and the observed vascular phenotypes

claim: Activating mutations of Tie2 have been linked to venous malformations in patients
source: Related to the findings of this study, activating mutations of Tie2 have been linked to venous malformations in patients (Vikkula et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Vikkula et al., 1996)

claim: Activation of wildtype Tie2 by its ligand Ang1 or VE-PTP inhibition has been shown to stabilize blood vasculature
source: Activation of wildtype Tie2 by its ligand Ang1 or VE-PTP inhibition, at least for a short period, has been shown to stabilize blood vasculature (Shen et al., 2014b)
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Shen et al., 2014b)

claim: Activating Tie2 mutations lead to venous malformations
source: while activating Tie2 mutations lead to venous malformations (Vikkula et al., 1996; Limaye et al., 2009; Boscolo et al., 2015).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Vikkula et al., 1996; Limaye et al., 2009; Boscolo et al., 2015)

claim: Tie2 deficiency led to embryonic lethality resulting from the defective vascular remodeling and heart development
source: Tie2 deficiency led to embryonic lethality resulting from the defective vascular remodeling and heart development (Dumont et al., 1994; Sato et al., 1995)
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Dumont et al., 1994; Sato et al., 1995)

claim: Combined deletion of Tie2 ligands Ang1 and Ang2 in mice was shown to disrupt Schlemm's canal formation leading to ocular hypertension and glaucoma
source: and combined deletion of Tie2 ligands Ang1 and Ang2 in mice was also shown to disrupt Schlemm's canal formation leading to ocular hypertension and glaucoma (Thomson et al., 2014).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Thomson et al., 2014)

claim: Patients with venous malformations were shown to have Tie2 missense point mutations
source: Patients with venous malformations were shown to have Tie2 missense point mutations (Vikkula et al., 1996), leading to ligand-independent Tie2 activation (Limaye et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (Vikkula et al., 1996; Limaye et al., 2009)

claim: Tie2 is essential for the specification of venous EC identity via the Akt mediated regulation of COUP-TFII protein stability
source: Findings from this study suggest that Tie2 is essential for the specification of venous EC identity via the Akt mediated regulation of COUP-TFII protein stability.
evidence: Inferred from the collective findings of the study

claim: COUP-TFII is a transcription factor expressed in venous but not arterial endothelial cells
source: COUP-TFII, a transcription factor expressed in venous but not arterial endothelial cells (ECs), has been shown to regulate venous identity via the inhibition of NOTCH mediated signals (You et al., 2005).
evidence: Supported by cited literature (You et al., 2005)
